lead.headline: Kampfgruppe takes Computer Gaming World’s first crown
lead.dek: Gary Grigsby’s tactical battlefield wins overall honors as computer bookkeeping makes a demanding wargame playable.
body: Computer Gaming World’s first annual awards have a clear winner: Kampfgruppe. The November–December issue names Strategic Simulations’ tactical World War II simulation its overall game of the year and its wargame-category winner. These are honors for an existing game, not a release announcement for this week.

Designer Gary Grigsby puts the fighting in Europe and gives players a random scenario generator as well as tactical problems to solve. The attraction is not simply a tank on the screen. A computer can shoulder line-of-sight calculations and opportunity-fire bookkeeping that would slow a comparable tabletop battle, leaving the commander to make decisions.

The magazine says Kampfgruppe led the voting throughout and finished substantially ahead of the closest non-wargame competitor, Ultima III. No numerical ballot total is supplied. SSI reports 8,000 copies sold and projects eventual sales of 25,000; that larger figure is a forecast, not a count already reached.

The other category awards show the range of the computer-game shelf: Ultima III wins adventure, Seven Cities of Gold takes strategy, and F-15 Strike Eagle receives action honors. The first ballot puts a demanding simulation at the head of a field that also embraces exploration, role-playing and flight.

stories.headline: The Bard’s Tale fills Skara Brae with music and danger
body: Electronic Arts and Interplay’s The Bard’s Tale receives a substantial Scorpia review in the November–December Computer Gaming World. Its product box lists Apple and a Commodore 64 edition for November at $44.95. That is the magazine’s availability listing, not independent confirmation of a particular shipping day.

Players recruit a party from several races and professions to challenge Mangar’s hold on Skara Brae. The bard’s music supplies a distinctive role in a world whose shops and dangers change between day and night.

Scorpia counts five dungeons and sixteen levels besides the town, making careful mapping a major part of the expedition. Three disks—Main, Dungeon and Character—carry the adventure. The promise is a substantial campaign, rather than a quick visit to a single maze.

stories.headline: QuantumLink brings color games to the Commodore connection
body: A Commodore 64 or 128 can become a graphical online meeting place in November’s COMPUTE! account of QuantumLink. Stephen Case of Quantum Computer Services describes a basic $9.95 monthly service, with some activities including communications time.

Special disk software holds graphics and sound for chess, backgammon and hangman. Bulletin boards, software previews, computer information, news and shopping extend the service beyond the game table. Chat and downloads add six cents a minute, or $3.60 an hour; the monthly subscription does not make every activity unlimited.

The report describes Uninet access and a year-end offer of terminal software and a free month, followed by a planned $25 signup fee after January 1. Launch-day accounts disagree, so this is November service coverage rather than a claim of a verified launch on a particular day this week.

stories.headline: PC Pursuit puts a flat fee against the long-distance bill
body: GTE Telenet is trying a different price proposition for hobbyists: $25 a month for evening and weekend access to distant bulletin boards, other computer users and noncommercial databases. November’s COMPUTE! describes a twelve-city experiment, not nationwide availability.

The network draws on capacity left idle after business hours, according to spokesperson Claudia Houston. A callback arrangement and automatic credit-card billing support the service. Expansion depends on the response to the trial.

A flat network charge can make a long session less alarming, but it does not erase a commercial information service’s own bill. CompuServe and The Source charges remain separate. For the BBS caller, the important comparison is a recurring network fee against an unpredictable long-distance telephone bill.

editorNote: Computer gaming awards lead the desk; graphical online play and flat-rate BBS experiments follow.
morningLine: Kampfgruppe takes the crown; Skara Brae beckons; the modem bill meets flat-rate experiments.

briefs.headline: User-group BBS discovery
briefs.summary: CGW’s telegaming survey points readers to local user groups and the P.A.M.S. BBS list via CompuServe GameSIG and The Source Member Publishing. It notes many free boards and some sysops charging $10–$30 yearly.

briefs.headline: Viewtron at home
briefs.summary: COMPUTE! p. 28 lists a $9.95 software starter kit including one free hour; later rates are nine cents/minute off-peak and 22 cents/minute daytime weekdays, with no monthly minimum or 1200-bps surcharge.

briefs.headline: Gato patrols the South Pacific
briefs.summary: COMPUTE! November review describes South Pacific submarine simulation with ten difficulty levels; Spectrum HoloByte; Apple/IBM $39.95, Macintosh $49.95.

market.headline: Online prices need two columns
market.summary: CGW’s 300-baud telegaming table quotes subscription/off-peak hourly charges of $29.95/$6 for CompuServe, $49.95/$8.40 for The Source, $49.95/$6 for Delphi and $39.95/$2 for PlayNet. Compare signup and usage charges separately; these are the table’s terms, not every promotional offer.

worldAnchor.headline: Siege devastates Bogotá’s Palace of Justice
worldAnchor.summary: M-19 seized the Palace of Justice on November 6; the military retook it during November 6–7. Fire and the assault killed hostages and members of the judiciary.

bbsNote.headline: Flat-rate experiments meet the telegaming boom
bbsNote.summary: November primary coverage documents both PC Pursuit’s limited $25 BBS network trial and QuantumLink’s Commodore-focused graphics service. Editorial desk notes below are sourced summaries, not invented verbatim BBS messages.

posts.text: Twelve-city evening/weekend trial: $25 monthly network access; commercial-service charges remain separate.
Special disk software supplies graphics and sound; chess, backgammon and hangman are described. Basic service $9.95 monthly; selected activities add six cents/minute.
CGW recommends the P.A.M.S. BBS list and user-group advice; free boards coexist with some $10–$30 annual memberships.

curiosity.headline: Read tomorrow’s science fiction over your modem
curiosity.summary: Baen Books lets online readers preview book chapters—and local BBSs may redistribute the files.
curiosity.detail: COMPUTE! November 1985 p. 20 reports Baen previews in CompuServe’s Science Fiction and Fantasy Forum. Files may be read, copied and distributed freely provided they are neither altered nor sold; local bulletin boards may retrieve and offer them without charge. Normal CompuServe connection charges still apply. This is a concrete early electronic-publishing experiment, not a claim that entire books are free.

Magazine cover dates establish monthly editorial context, not exact on-sale, shipment or announcement days. CGW is a combined November–December issue; date its awards and review to that issue rather than a fabricated day.

Games are editorial selections, not a sales ranking. Music uses Billboard Top Rock Tracks November 9; movies use November 8–10 weekend receipts.
SSI’s 25,000 sales figure is a projection; 8,000 is the reported achieved total.
